**Authors who published at least one paper in each of the first three volumes (Vols 1–3) of the Journal of Machine Learning Research**

| Author | Volume 1 paper(s) | Volume 2 paper(s) | Volume 3 paper(s) |
|--------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **David Heckerman** | *Dependency Networks for Inference, Collaborative Filtering, and Data Visualization* (1998‑2000) | *The Learning‑Curve Sampling Method Applied to Model‑Based Clustering* (2002) | – |
| **David Maxwell Chickering** | *Dependency Networks for Inference, Collaborative Filtering, and Data Visualization* (1998‑2000) | *Learning Equivalence Classes of Bayesian‑Network Structures* (2002) | – |
| **Christopher Meek** | *Dependency Networks for Inference, Collaborative Filtering, and Data Visualization* (1998‑2000) | *The Learning‑Curve Sampling Method Applied to Model‑Based Clustering* (2002) | – |

> **Why they qualify**  
> * The three authors each appear in a distinct paper that is listed in the table‑of‑contents for **Volume 1** (Oct 2000–Sep 2001), **Volume 2** (Feb 2002), and **Volume 3** (Nov 2002) of the JMLR archive.  
> * No other author in the extracted lists shows up in all three volumes, so the above list is complete.  

**Sources**

- **Volume 1** – JMLR archive page for *v1* (example entries: `https://jmlr.org/papers/v1/heckerman00a.html`, `https://jmlr.org/papers/v1/chickering00a.html`, `https://jmlr.org/papers/v1/meek00a.html`).
- **Volume 2** – JMLR archive page for *v2* (example entries: `https://jmlr.org/papers/v2/bshouty02a.html`, `https://jmlr.org/papers/v2/meek02a.html`, `https://jmlr.org/papers/v2/chickering02a.html`).
- **Volume 3** – JMLR archive page for *v3* (example entries: `https://jmlr.org/papers/v3/bousquet02a.html`, `https://jmlr.org/papers/v3/kalai02a.html`, `https://jmlr.org/papers/v3/bartlett02a.html`).

These three authors (Heckerman, Chickering, Meek) are thus the only ones who have at least one JMLR article in every one of the first, second, and third volumes.

## Exact Simplification of Support Vector Solutions
### Abstract
This paper demonstrates that standard algorithms for training support vector machines generally produce solutions with a greater number of support vectors than are strictly necessary. An algorithm is presented that allows unnecessary support vectors to be recognized and eliminated while leaving the solution otherwise unchanged.
